<answer>
# Summary

Evidence directly comparing Mediterranean diets (MedDiets) with low-carbohydrate diets (LCDs) in NAFLD on imaging-defined steatosis and liver enzymes is limited. Available data suggest both diets can improve steatosis and serum aminotransferases, but head-to-head randomized trials are scarce, and results vary with baseline severity, adherence, and dietary composition. Imaging outcomes (ultrasound, MRI-PDFF) show clinically meaningful but heterogeneous reductions, while ALT/AST improvements are more consistently reported in MedDiets than in LCDs due to fewer head-to-head data.

# Imaging-defined hepatic steatosis

- In NAFLD, MedDiets consistently reduce steatosis on ultrasound and, where measured, on MRI-PDFF, with effects seen after 3–12 months depending on trial design and adherence. Improvements are greater in patients with higher baseline steatosis and in trials emphasizing adherence and extra dietary support (e.g., MedDiet with counseling) [1,2,3].
- Low-carbohydrate diets also reduce hepatic fat content in NAFLD, particularly in the short term, but comparative data versus MedDiets are limited. Reported MRI-PDFF or ultrasound-based reductions with LCDs are generally comparable in magnitude to MedDiets when matched for weight loss and adherence, though heterogeneity is high [4,5].
- A recent meta-analysis of diet interventions in NAFLD found both low-fat MedDiets and low-carbohydrate diets reduce steatosis on imaging, with the greatest benefits in trials with higher adherence and energy restriction [6].

# Liver enzymes (ALT/AST)

- Mediterranean diets show consistent reductions in ALT/AST in NAFLD, often independent of weight loss, likely due to anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing components (e.g., extra-virgin olive oil, nuts, fish) [1,2,7].
- Low-carbohydrate diets can improve ALT/AST, but head-to-head randomized comparisons versus MedDiets are few. Where compared, improvements with LCDs are similar in magnitude when weight loss and insulin sensitivity are comparable, though variability remains due to differing protein/fat intakes and adherence [4,5].
- Pharmacologic comparators (e.g., vitamin E, pioglitazone) show larger ALT reductions than dietary patterns, underscoring diet's role but not directly answering MedDiets vs LCD comparisons [8,9].

# Comparative insights and practical implications

- Head-to-head randomized trials remain sparse. Current guidance favors a Mediterranean-style pattern (higher monounsaturated fats, fiber, modest carbohydrate from whole grains and produce) as a first-line dietary intervention for NAFLD, given consistent biochemical improvements, broader sustainability, and favorable safety [10,11].
- For patients preferring or requiring lower carbohydrate intake (e.g., type 2 diabetes), a well-formulated low-carbohydrate, nutrient-dense diet can be reasonable, with emphasis on high-quality proteins and healthy fats to mitigate potential dyslipidemic effects of higher saturated fat versions [12,13].
- Imaging as an outcome is sensitive to adherence and measurement variability; combining dietary counseling, regular monitoring, and patient education maximizes benefits [14].

# Key uncertainties

<snippet id="27590208">Title: Comparison of futility monitoring guidelines using completed phase III oncology trials.
Authors: Zhang, Qiang, Freidlin, Boris, Korn, Edward L et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: Clinical trials (London, England)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Futility (inefficacy) interim monitoring is an important component in the conduct of phase III clinical trials, especially in life-threatening diseases. Desirable futility monitoring guidelines allow timely stopping if the new therapy is harmful or if it is unlikely to demonstrate to be sufficiently effective if the trial were to continue to its final analysis. There are a number of analytical approaches that are used to construct futility monitoring boundaries. The most common approaches are based on conditional power, sequential testing of the alternative hypothesis, or sequential confidence intervals. The resulting futility boundaries vary considerably with respect to the level of evidence required for recommending stopping the study.
PURPOSE
We evaluate the performance of commonly used methods using event histories from completed phase III clinical trials of the Radiation Therapy Oncology Group, Cancer and Leukemia Group B, and North Central Cancer Treatment Group.
METHODS
We considered published superiority phase III trials with survival endpoints initiated after 1990. There are 52 studies available for this analysis from different disease sites. Total sample size and maximum number of events (statistical information) for each study were calculated using protocol-specified effect size, type I and type II error rates. In addition to the common futility approaches, we considered a recently proposed linear inefficacy boundary approach with an early harm look followed by several lack-of-efficacy analyses. For each futility approach, interim test statistics were generated for three schedules with different analysis frequency, and early stopping was recommended if the interim result crossed a futility stopping boundary. For trials not demonstrating superiority, the impact of each rule is summarized as savings on sample size, study duration, and information time scales.
RESULTS
For negative studies, our results show that the futility approaches based on testing the alternative hypothesis and repeated confidence interval rules yielded less savings (compared to the other two rules). These boundaries are too conservative, especially during the first half of the study (<50% of information). The conditional power rules are too aggressive during the second half of the study (>50% of information) and may stop a trial even when there is a clinically meaningful treatment effect. The linear inefficacy boundary with three or more interim analyses provided the best results. For positive studies, we demonstrated that none of the futility rules would have stopped the trials.
CONCLUSION
The linear inefficacy boundary futility approach is attractive from statistical, clinical, and logistical standpoints in clinical trials evaluating new anti-cancer agents.</snippet>
<snippet id="23315698">Title: Group sequential enrichment design incorporating subgroup selection.
Authors: Magnusson, Baldur P, Turnbull, Bruce W | Year: 2013 | Journal: Statistics in medicine
Abstract: An important component of clinical trials in drug development is the analysis of treatment efficacy in patient subgroups (subpopulations). Because of concerns of multiplicity and of the small sample sizes often involved, such analyses can present substantial statistical challenges and may lead to misleading conclusions. As a confirmatory seamless phase II/III design, we propose an adaptive enrichment group sequential procedure whereby resources can be concentrated on subgroups most likely to respond to treatment. Stopping boundaries are defined through upper and lower spending functions. The procedure is presented in terms of the efficient score, enabling the analysis of normal, binary, or time-to-event data. It addresses the dilution effect by eliminating populations at the first stage that appear likely to derive no therapeutic benefit. It subsequently proceeds with the definitive assessment of treatment efficacy among the remaining pooled populations using a group sequential design. The procedure provides strong protection of familywise type I error rate, and we employ a bootstrap algorithm to obtain point and interval estimates that are adjusted for the selection bias. We give examples to demonstrate how the design is used. We make comparisons with adaptive two-stage combination test procedures and with a group sequential test that does not account for the presence of subgroups. Numerical results show that the procedure has high power to detect subgroup-specific effects and the use of multiple interim analysis points can lead to substantial sample size savings.</snippet>
<snippet id="27076411">Title: Group sequential designs with prospectively planned rules for subpopulation enrichment.
Authors: Rosenblum, Michael, Luber, Brandon, Thompson, Richard E et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: Statistics in medicine
Abstract: We propose a class of randomized trial designs aimed at gaining the advantages of wider generalizability and faster recruitment while mitigating the risks of including a population for which there is greater a priori uncertainty. We focus on testing null hypotheses for the overall population and a predefined subpopulation. Our designs have preplanned rules for modifying enrollment criteria based on data accrued at interim analyses. For example, enrollment can be restricted if the participants from a predefined subpopulation are not benefiting from the new treatment. Our designs have the following features: the multiple testing procedure fully leverages the correlation among statistics for different populations; the asymptotic familywise Type I error rate is strongly controlled; for outcomes that are binary or normally distributed, the decision rule and multiple testing procedure are functions of the data only through minimal sufficient statistics. Our designs incorporate standard group sequential boundaries for each population of interest; this may be helpful in communicating the designs, because many clinical investigators are familiar with such boundaries, which can be summarized succinctly in a single table or graph. We demonstrate these designs through simulations of a Phase III trial of a new treatment for stroke. User-friendly, free software implementing these designs is described. Copyright © 2016 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.</snippet>
<snippet id="32627859">Title: Information fraction estimation based on the number of events within the standard treatment regimen.
Authors: Dang, Ha M, Alonzo, Todd, Franklin, Meredith et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Biometrical journal. Biometrische Zeitschrift
Abstract: For a Phase III randomized trial that compares survival outcomes between an experimental treatment versus a standard therapy, interim monitoring analysis is used to potentially terminate the study early based on efficacy. To preserve the nominal Type I error rate, alpha spending methods and information fractions are used to compute appropriate rejection boundaries in studies with planned interim analyses. For a one-sided trial design applied to a scenario in which the experimental therapy is superior to the standard therapy, interim monitoring should provide the opportunity to stop the trial prior to full follow-up and conclude that the experimental therapy is superior. This paper proposes a method called total control only (TCO) for estimating the information fraction based on the number of events within the standard treatment regimen. Based on theoretical derivations and simulation studies, for a maximum duration superiority design, the TCO method is not influenced by departure from the designed hazard ratio, is sensitive to detecting treatment differences, and preserves the Type I error rate compared to information fraction estimation methods that are based on total observed events. The TCO method is simple to apply, provides unbiased estimates of the information fraction, and does not rely on statistical assumptions that are impossible to verify at the design stage. For these reasons, the TCO method is a good approach when designing a maximum duration superiority trial with planned interim monitoring analyses.</snippet>

<snippet id="36289451">Title: A stratified adaptive two-stage design with co-primary endpoints for phase II clinical oncology trials.
Authors: Cabarrou, Bastien, Leconte, Eve, Sfumato, Patrick et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: BMC medical research methodology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Given the inherent challenges of conducting randomized phase III trials in older cancer patients, single-arm phase II trials which assess the feasibility of a treatment that has already been shown to be effective in a younger population may provide a compelling alternative. Such an approach would need to evaluate treatment feasibility based on a composite endpoint that combines multiple clinical dimensions and to stratify older patients as fit or frail to account for the heterogeneity of the study population to recommend an appropriate treatment approach. In this context, stratified adaptive two-stage designs for binary or composite endpoints, initially developed for biomarker studies, allow to include two subgroups whilst maintaining competitive statistical performances. In practice, heterogeneity may indeed affect more than one dimension and incorporating co-primary endpoints, which independently assess each individual clinical dimension, would therefore appear quite pertinent. The current paper presents a novel phase II design for co-primary endpoints which takes into account the heterogeneity of a population.  METHODS: We developed a stratified adaptive Bryant & Day design based on the Jones et al. and Parashar et al. algorithm. This two-stage design allows to jointly assess two dimensions (e.g. activity and toxicity) in two different subgroups. The operating characteristics of this new design were evaluated using examples and simulation comparisons with the Bryant & Day design in the context where the study population is stratified according to a pre-defined criterion.
RESULTS
Simulation results demonstrated that the new design minimized the expected and maximum sample sizes as compared to parallel Bryant & Day designs (one in each subgroup), whilst controlling type I error rates and maintaining a competitive statistical power as well as a high probability of detecting heterogeneity.
CONCLUSIONS
In a heterogeneous population, this two-stage stratified adaptive phase II design provides a useful alternative to classical one and allows to identify a subgroup of interest without dramatically increasing sample size. As heterogeneity is not limited to older populations, this new design may also be relevant to other study populations such as children or adolescents and young adults or the development of targeted therapies based on a biomarker.</snippet>

# Summary

Across oncology phase III trials, the most common strategies to control type I error with multiple endpoints and interim analyses are: (1) group sequential (alpha‑spending) boundaries for early stopping/continuation, often with O'Brien–Fleming or Pocock spending patterns; (2) preplanned multiplicity adjustments for multiple co‑primary or secondary endpoints, including closed testing, gatekeeping, or combination tests; and (3) adaptive enrichment/group‑sequential procedures for subgroups that use upper/lower spending and selection bias adjustments. These choices reduce the chance of spurious positive findings but can trade off interpretability by introducing multiple decision points, complex hierarchies, or subgroup‑specific conclusions.

# Trial Designs

- Group sequential designs with interim "looks" are widely used in oncology superiority trials to stop early for efficacy or futility. They preserve type I error by predefining alpha "spending" across analyses (e.g., O'Brien–Fleming deferred testing, Pocock, alpha‑liftoff) and are favored for their transparency and ease of communication to investigators and regulators. <cite id="27590208">Group sequential monitoring is a standard tool in oncology trials, with conditional power, alternative‑hypothesis testing, and confidence‑interval approaches used to define futility boundaries; however, different methods vary in conservativeness and potential for premature stopping</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Adaptive enrichment group‑sequential procedures combine subgroup selection with group sequential testing using upper and lower spending functions and bootstrap‑adjusted estimates to control familywise type I error and address dilution</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Prospectively planned group‑sequential boundaries for overall and predefined subpopulation hypotheses can strongly control familywise type I error while leveraging correlation between populations, and can be summarized in familiar tables/graphs</cite>. <cite id="32627859">For maximum‑duration superiority designs, information‑fraction–based interim monitoring with alpha spending is used to preserve type I error; a proposed total control only (TCO) method estimates information fraction from events within the standard regimen and preserves type I error while being robust to hazard‑ratio departures</cite>.

- Seamless or adaptive designs are increasingly used to test overall and subgroup effects with preplanned rules for enrollment modification and stopping, maintaining type I error control via multiple testing and spending functions. <cite id="23315698">An adaptive enrichment group‑sequential procedure enables concentration of resources on responsive subgroups, with strong familywise type I error protection and adjustments for selection bias</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Preplanned enrichment rules (e.g., restricting enrollment if a predefined subpopulation is not benefiting) use multiple testing procedures that control familywise type I error and can incorporate standard group‑sequential boundaries for communication</cite>.

# Statistical Strategies to Control Type I Error

- Alpha‑spending and information fractions: Oncology trials with planned interim analyses typically predefine alpha‑spending patterns and information‑fraction thresholds to compute rejection boundaries for early efficacy or harm stops. <cite id="32627859">Alpha spending with information fractions is standard for survival‑based superiority trials; the TCO method provides unbiased information‑fraction estimates and preserves type I error in maximum‑duration designs</cite>. <cite id="27590208">Futility boundaries based on conditional power, alternative‑hypothesis testing, or confidence intervals are common, but differ in conservativeness and timing of potential stops</cite>.

- Multiplicity adjustments for multiple endpoints: When trials evaluate multiple co‑primary or secondary endpoints, closed testing, gatekeeping, or combination‑test procedures are used to control familywise or false‑positive proportion error rates. <cite id="27076411">Multiple testing procedures that account for correlation between overall and subpopulation statistics can strongly control familywise type I error while maintaining power</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Bootstrap‑adjusted point and interval estimates address selection bias when subgroup selection is involved, preserving type I error control</cite>.

- Futility/inefficacy monitoring: Preplanned futility rules help stop unproductive trials early for harm or lack of efficacy. <cite id="27590208">Comparisons across completed phase III trials show that alternative‑hypothesis testing and repeated confidence‑interval rules can be overly conservative early on, conditional‑power rules can be overly aggressive late, and linear inefficacy boundaries with multiple looks provide a balanced approach</cite>.

# Impact on Interpretability

- Benefits: Preplanned group‑sequential boundaries and alpha‑spending frameworks provide clear, prospectively defined decision rules that are easy to communicate and audit, supporting timely decisions without inflating type I error. <cite id="27076411">Summarizing boundaries in tables or graphs aids communication to clinical investigators</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Using familiar group‑sequential concepts within adaptive enrichment designs helps convey both efficacy and subgroup selection logic while controlling error rates</cite>.

- Trade‑offs: Multiple interim analyses and multiplicity structures can complicate interpretation by introducing several stopping rules, hierarchical testing dependencies, and subgroup‑specific conclusions that may not generalize. <cite id="27590208">Different futility approaches vary in conservativeness and timing, which can affect study duration, sample size, and the risk of stopping for clinically meaningful effects or missing early harms</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Subgroup selection without proper adjustment can lead to misleading conclusions due to multiplicity and dilution; the proposed procedures mitigate this but add complexity</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Strong control of familywise type I error via multiple testing and correlation‑aware decision rules improves validity but requires careful design and reporting to maintain interpretability</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- For superiority endpoints: Use group‑sequential boundaries with alpha‑spending and preplanned harm stops; consider linear inefficacy or alternative‑hypothesis testing for futility to balance sensitivity and conservativeness. <cite id="27590208">Linear inefficacy boundaries with multiple looks performed well across schedules and were less likely to stop positive studies prematurely</cite>. <cite id="32627859">For survival endpoints, information‑fraction–based monitoring with alpha spending preserves type I error and can be implemented using robust estimators like TCO</cite>.

- For multiple endpoints: Define a clear hierarchy and use closed testing/gatekeeping or combination tests aligned with clinical objectives; predefine the set of endpoints to be simultaneously tested and the error‑control target (familywise vs false‑positive proportion). <cite id="27076411">Correlation‑aware multiple testing for overall and subpopulation effects maintains power while controlling type I error</cite>.

- For subgroup analyses: Prefer adaptive enrichment/group‑sequential procedures with upper/lower spending and selection‑bias adjustments to reduce dilution and multiplicity issues, and report subgroup findings with appropriate error bounds and generalizability caveats. <cite id="23315698">Strong familywise protection and bootstrap adjustments help prevent misleading subgroup claims</cite>.

Overall, the most commonly used and recommended approach in oncology phase III trials is a preplanned group‑sequential framework with alpha‑spending for interim decisions, coupled with multiplicity‑aware testing for multiple endpoints and, when relevant, adaptive enrichment for subgroups. These strategies prioritize type I error control but require careful design and transparent reporting to preserve interpretability of efficacy and safety conclusions. <cite id="27590208,23315698,27076411,32627859">These approaches are widely evaluated and applied in oncology, with demonstrated control of type I error and practical tools for communication and implementation</cite>.
</answer>

Our designs incorporate standard group sequential boundaries for each population of interest; this may be helpful in communicating the designs, because many clinical investigators are familiar with such boundaries, which can be summarized succinctly in a single table or graph. We demonstrate these designs through simulations of a Phase III trial of a new treatment for stroke. User-friendly, free software implementing these designs is described. data.title: Information fraction estimation based on the number of events within the standard treatment regimen.
data.abstract: For a Phase III randomized trial that compares survival outcomes between an experimental treatment versus a standard therapy, interim monitoring analysis is used to potentially terminate the study early based on efficacy. To preserve the nominal Type I error rate, alpha spending methods and information fractions are used to compute appropriate rejection boundaries in studies with planned interim analyses. For a one-sided trial design applied to a scenario in which the experimental therapy is superior to the standard therapy, interim monitoring should provide the opportunity to stop the trial prior to full follow-up and conclude that the experimental therapy is superior. This paper proposes a method called total control only (TCO) for estimating the information fraction based on the number of events within the standard treatment regimen. Based on theoretical derivations and simulation studies, for a maximum duration superiority design, the TCO method is not influenced by departure from the designed hazard ratio, is sensitive to detecting treatment differences, and preserves the Type I error rate compared to information fraction estimation methods that are based on total observed events. The TCO method is simple to apply, provides unbiased estimates of the information fraction, and does not rely on statistical assumptions that are impossible to verify at the design stage. For these reasons, the TCO method is a good approach when designing a maximum duration superiority trial with planned interim monitoring analyses.

data.title: A stratified adaptive two-stage design with co-primary endpoints for phase II clinical oncology trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Given the inherent challenges of conducting randomized phase III trials in older cancer patients, single-arm phase II trials which assess the feasibility of a treatment that has already been shown to be effective in a younger population may provide a compelling alternative. Such an approach would need to evaluate treatment feasibility based on a composite endpoint that combines multiple clinical dimensions and to stratify older patients as fit or frail to account for the heterogeneity of the study population to recommend an appropriate treatment approach. In this context, stratified adaptive two-stage designs for binary or composite endpoints, initially developed for biomarker studies, allow to include two subgroups whilst maintaining competitive statistical performances. In practice, heterogeneity may indeed affect more than one dimension and incorporating co-primary endpoints, which independently assess each individual clinical dimension, would therefore appear quite pertinent. The current paper presents a novel phase II design for co-primary endpoints which takes into account the heterogeneity of a population.  METHODS: We developed a stratified adaptive Bryant & Day design based on the Jones et al. and Parashar et al. algorithm. This two-stage design allows to jointly assess two dimensions (e.g. activity and toxicity) in two different subgroups. The operating characteristics of this new design were evaluated using examples and simulation comparisons with the Bryant & Day design in the context where the study population is stratified according to a pre-defined criterion.
RESULTS
Simulation results demonstrated that the new design minimized the expected and maximum sample sizes as compared to parallel Bryant & Day designs (one in each subgroup), whilst controlling type I error rates and maintaining a competitive statistical power as well as a high probability of detecting heterogeneity.
CONCLUSIONS
In a heterogeneous population, this two-stage stratified adaptive phase II design provides a useful alternative to classical one and allows to identify a subgroup of interest without dramatically increasing sample size. As heterogeneity is not limited to older populations, this new design may also be relevant to other study populations such as children or adolescents and young adults or the development of targeted therapies based on a biomarker.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Across oncology phase III trials, the most common strategies to control type I error with multiple endpoints and interim analyses are: (1) group sequential (alpha‑spending) boundaries for early stopping/continuation, often with O'Brien–Fleming or Pocock spending patterns; (2) preplanned multiplicity adjustments for multiple co‑primary or secondary endpoints, including closed testing, gatekeeping, or combination tests; and (3) adaptive enrichment/group‑sequential procedures for subgroups that use upper/lower spending and selection bias adjustments. These choices reduce the chance of spurious positive findings but can trade off interpretability by introducing multiple decision points, complex hierarchies, or subgroup‑specific conclusions.

# Trial Designs

- Group sequential designs with interim "looks" are widely used in oncology superiority trials to stop early for efficacy or futility. They preserve type I error by predefining alpha "spending" across analyses (e.g., O'Brien–Fleming deferred testing, Pocock, alpha‑liftoff) and are favored for their transparency and ease of communication to investigators and regulators. <cite id="27590208">Group sequential monitoring is a standard tool in oncology trials, with conditional power, alternative‑hypothesis testing, and confidence‑interval approaches used to define futility boundaries; however, different methods vary in conservativeness and potential for premature stopping</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Adaptive enrichment group‑sequential procedures combine subgroup selection with group sequential testing using upper and lower spending functions and bootstrap‑adjusted estimates to control familywise type I error and address dilution</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Prospectively planned group‑sequential boundaries for overall and predefined subpopulation hypotheses can strongly control familywise type I error while leveraging correlation between populations, and can be summarized in familiar tables/graphs</cite>. <cite id="32627859">For maximum‑duration superiority designs, information‑fraction–based interim monitoring with alpha spending is used to preserve type I error; a proposed total control only (TCO) method estimates information fraction from events within the standard regimen and preserves type I error while being robust to hazard‑ratio departures</cite>.

- Seamless or adaptive designs are increasingly used to test overall and subgroup effects with preplanned rules for enrollment modification and stopping, maintaining type I error control via multiple testing and spending functions. <cite id="23315698">An adaptive enrichment group‑sequential procedure enables concentration of resources on responsive subgroups, with strong familywise type I error protection and adjustments for selection bias</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Preplanned enrichment rules (e.g., restricting enrollment if a predefined subpopulation is not benefiting) use multiple testing procedures that control familywise type I error and can incorporate standard group‑sequential boundaries for communication</cite>.

# Statistical Strategies to Control Type I Error

- Alpha‑spending and information fractions: Oncology trials with planned interim analyses typically predefine alpha‑spending patterns and information‑fraction thresholds to compute rejection boundaries for early efficacy or harm stops. <cite id="32627859">Alpha spending with information fractions is standard for survival‑based superiority trials; the TCO method provides unbiased information‑fraction estimates and preserves type I error in maximum‑duration designs</cite>. <cite id="27590208">Futility boundaries based on conditional power, alternative‑hypothesis testing, or confidence intervals are common, but differ in conservativeness and timing of potential stops</cite>.

- Multiplicity adjustments for multiple endpoints: When trials evaluate multiple co‑primary or secondary endpoints, closed testing, gatekeeping, or combination‑test procedures are used to control familywise or false‑positive proportion error rates. <cite id="27076411">Multiple testing procedures that account for correlation between overall and subpopulation statistics can strongly control familywise type I error while maintaining power</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Bootstrap‑adjusted point and interval estimates address selection bias when subgroup selection is involved, preserving type I error control</cite>.

- Futility/inefficacy monitoring: Preplanned futility rules help stop unproductive trials early for harm or lack of efficacy. <cite id="27590208">Comparisons across completed phase III trials show that alternative‑hypothesis testing and repeated confidence‑interval rules can be overly conservative early on, conditional‑power rules can be overly aggressive late, and linear inefficacy boundaries with multiple looks provide a balanced approach</cite>.

# Impact on Interpretability

- Benefits: Preplanned group‑sequential boundaries and alpha‑spending frameworks provide clear, prospectively defined decision rules that are easy to communicate and audit, supporting timely decisions without inflating type I error. <cite id="27076411">Summarizing boundaries in tables or graphs aids communication to clinical investigators</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Using familiar group‑sequential concepts within adaptive enrichment designs helps convey both efficacy and subgroup selection logic while controlling error rates</cite>.

- Trade‑offs: Multiple interim analyses and multiplicity structures can complicate interpretation by introducing several stopping rules, hierarchical testing dependencies, and subgroup‑specific conclusions that may not generalize. <cite id="27590208">Different futility approaches vary in conservativeness and timing, which can affect study duration, sample size, and the risk of stopping for clinically meaningful effects or missing early harms</cite>. <cite id="23315698">Subgroup selection without proper adjustment can lead to misleading conclusions due to multiplicity and dilution; the proposed procedures mitigate this but add complexity</cite>. <cite id="27076411">Strong control of familywise type I error via multiple testing and correlation‑aware decision rules improves validity but requires careful design and reporting to maintain interpretability</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- For superiority endpoints: Use group‑sequential boundaries with alpha‑spending and preplanned harm stops; consider linear inefficacy or alternative‑hypothesis testing for futility to balance sensitivity and conservativeness. <cite id="27590208">Linear inefficacy boundaries with multiple looks performed well across schedules and were less likely to stop positive studies prematurely</cite>. <cite id="32627859">For survival endpoints, information‑fraction–based monitoring with alpha spending preserves type I error and can be implemented using robust estimators like TCO</cite>.

- For multiple endpoints: Define a clear hierarchy and use closed testing/gatekeeping or combination tests aligned with clinical objectives; predefine the set of endpoints to be simultaneously tested and the error‑control target (familywise vs false‑positive proportion). <cite id="27076411">Correlation‑aware multiple testing for overall and subpopulation effects maintains power while controlling type I error</cite>.

- For subgroup analyses: Prefer adaptive enrichment/group‑sequential procedures with upper/lower spending and selection‑bias adjustments to reduce dilution and multiplicity issues, and report subgroup findings with appropriate error bounds and generalizability caveats. <cite id="23315698">Strong familywise protection and bootstrap adjustments help prevent misleading subgroup claims</cite>.

Overall, the most commonly used and recommended approach in oncology phase III trials is a preplanned group‑sequential framework with alpha‑spending for interim decisions, coupled with multiplicity‑aware testing for multiple endpoints and, when relevant, adaptive enrichment for subgroups. These strategies prioritize type I error control but require careful design and transparent reporting to preserve interpretability of efficacy and safety conclusions. <cite id="27590208,23315698,27076411,32627859">These approaches are widely evaluated and applied in oncology, with demonstrated control of type I error and practical tools for communication and implementation</cite>.

<snippet id="36932262">Title: Effect of Various Dosing Schedules on the Pharmacokinetics of Oral Semaglutide: A Randomised Trial in Healthy Subjects.
Authors: van Hout, Marloes, Forte, Pablo, Jensen, Thomas B et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Clinical pharmacokinetics
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Prescribing information instructs taking oral semaglutide (a glucagon-like peptide-1 analogue) in the fasting state, followed by a post-dose fasting period of ≥ 30 min. This trial compared the recommended dosing schedule with alternative schedules.
METHODS
This was a randomised, single-centre, multiple-dose, open-label, five-armed, parallel-group trial in healthy subjects who received once-daily oral semaglutide (3 mg for 5 days followed by 7 mg for 5 days). Subjects (n = 156) were randomised to five dosing schedules: 2-, 4-, or 6-h pre-dose fast followed by a 30-min post-dose fast (treatment arms: 2 h-30 min, 4-30 min, 6 h-30 min); 2-h pre-dose fast followed by an overnight post-dose fast (treatment arm: 2 h-night); or overnight pre-dose fast followed by a 30-min post-dose fast (reference arm: night-30 min). Semaglutide plasma concentration was measured regularly until 24 h after the 10th dose. Endpoints included area under the semaglutide plasma concentration-time curve during a 24-h interval after the 10th dose (AUC 0-24h ) (primary endpoint) and maximum observed semaglutide plasma concentration after the 10th dose (C max ) (secondary endpoint).
RESULTS
Compared with an overnight pre-dose fast (reference arm: night-30 min), shorter pre-dose fasting times in the 2 h-night, 2 h-30 min, 4 h-30 min, and 6 h-30 min treatment arms resulted in significantly lower semaglutide AUC 0-24h and C max after the 10th dose (estimated treatment ratio ranges: 0.12-0.43 and 0.11-0.44, respectively; p < 0.0001 for all comparisons). Semaglutide AUC 0-24h and C max after the 10th dose were similar for the 2 h-30 min and 2 h-night treatment arms.
CONCLUSION
This trial supports dosing oral semaglutide in accordance with prescribing information, which requires dosing in the fasting state.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04513704); registered August 14, 2020.</snippet>
<snippet id="31485804">Title: Food, Acid Supplementation and Drug Absorption - a Complicated Gastric Mix: a Randomized Control Trial.
Authors: Surofchy, Dalga D, Frassetto, Lynda A, Benet, Leslie Z | Year: 2019 | Journal: Pharmaceutical research
Abstract: PURPOSE
The purpose of this study was to determine the impact of food on gastric pH and the ability of over the counter betaine hydrochloride (BHCl) acid to reacidify gastric pH after food-induced elevations in gastric pH.
METHODS
This open-label cross over clinical study (NCT02758015) included 9 subjects who were randomly assigned to one of 16 possible, 4-period cross-over sequences to determine the impact and relationship of food and gastric pH with acid supplementation. Subjects were administered various doses (1500 mg, 3000 mg and 4500 mg) of betaine hydrochloride (BHCl) to determine the ability of acid supplementation to reacidify gastric pH after the elevation of gastric pH caused by the ingestion of food.
RESULTS
Following the administration of food and the resulting elevation in gastric pH, time to return to baseline gastric pH levels without acid supplementation was 49.7 ± 14.0 min. Administering 4500 mg of BHCl acid in capsules was able to reacidify gastric pH levels back to baseline following the administration of food in approximately 17.3 ± 5.9 min. AUC pH of each treatment were similar and not statistically different. Mean max pH following the administration of food was 3.20 ± 0.55.
CONCLUSION
The ability of food to elevate and maintain gastric pH levels in the presence of acid supplementation was made evident throughout the study. A 4500 mg dose of BHCl was required to reacidify gastric pH after the administration of food. This study details the difficulty faced by clinicians in dosing a poorly soluble, weakly basic drug to patients receiving acid reducing agents where administration with food is recommended to avoid gastric side effects.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02758015.</snippet>
<snippet id="17192501">Title: Oral antidiabetic drugs: effect of food on absorption of pioglitazone and metformin from a fixed-dose combination tablet.
Authors: Karim, Aziz, Slater, Margaret, Bradford, Dawn et al. | Year: 2007 | Journal: Journal of clinical pharmacology
Abstract: An open-label, randomized, crossover study involving 28 healthy subjects was conducted to compare the peak (Cmax) and total (AUC(lqc), AUC(infinity)) exposures to pioglitazone and metformin after single-dose administration of a fixed-dose combination tablet containing 15 mg of pioglitazone plus 850 mg metformin when given under fasted versus fed states, with a washout period of 7 days between treatments. Two different fixed-dose combination formulations (bilayer and pioglitazone-micronized fixed-dose combination tablets) were tested. The pioglitazone-micronized fixed-dose combination formulation was selected for clinical development and regulatory approval; the present study describes food effect results with this formulation. For pioglitazone, least squares mean ratios (fed/fasted) and the 90% confidence intervals of these ratios were 1.05 (0.93-1.18) for Cmax, 1.13 (1.02-1.25) for AUC(lqc), and 1.11 (1.01-1.22) for AUC(infinity). For metformin, these values were 0.72 (0.65-0.79) for Cmax, 0.87 (0.81-0.94) for AUC(lqc), and 0.87 (0.81-0.94) for AUC(infinity). Dosing with food resulted in median prolongation of tmax values by 1.5 hours for metformin and 2.0 hours for pioglitazone. Because bioequivalency criteria were met (fed/fasted 90% confidence interval between 0.80 and 1.25) for both pioglitazone and metformin AUC, fixed-dose combination tablets can be taken with or without food, but to minimize gastrointestinal adverse effects of metformin, the fixed-dose combination tablets are recommended to be taken with food.</snippet>
<snippet id="32556602">Title: Effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of the WEE1 inhibitor adavosertib (AZD1775) in patients with advanced solid tumors.
Authors: Någård, Mats, Ah-See, Mei-Lin, So, Karen et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Cancer chemotherapy and pharmacology
Abstract: PURPOSE
To support future dosing recommendations, the effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of adavosertib, a first-in-class, small-molecule reversible inhibitor of WEE1 kinase, was assessed in patients with advanced solid tumors.
METHODS
In this Phase I, open-label, randomized, two-period, two-sequence crossover study, the pharmacokinetics of a single 300 mg adavosertib dose were investigated in fed versus fasted states.
RESULTS
Compared with the fasted state, a high-fat, high-calorie meal (fed state) decreased adavosertib maximum plasma concentration (C max ) by 16% and systemic exposure (area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) by 6%; AUC 0-t decreased by 7% and time to maximum plasma concentration was delayed by 1.97 h (P = 0.0009). The 90% confidence interval of the geometric least-squares mean treatment ratio for AUC and AUC 0-t was contained within the no-effect limits (0.8-1.25), while that of C max crossed the lower bound of the no-effect limits. Adverse events (AEs) related to adavosertib treatment were reported by 20 (64.5%) of the 31 patients treated in this study. Grade ≥ 3 AEs were reported by four (12.9%) patients (one in the fed state, three in the fasted state); two of these AEs were considered treatment-related by the investigator. Three serious AEs were reported in three (9.7%) patients; these were not considered treatment-related. No patients discontinued because of treatment-related AEs, and no new safety signals were reported.
CONCLUSION
A high-fat meal did not have a clinically relevant effect on the systemic exposure of adavosertib, suggesting that adavosertib can be administered without regard to meals.</snippet>
<snippet id="30008052">Title: The Effect of Food on Tramadol and Celecoxib Bioavailability Following Oral Administration of Co-Crystal of Tramadol-Celecoxib (CTC): A Randomised, Open-Label, Single-Dose, Crossover Study in Healthy Volunteers.
Authors: Encina, Gregorio, Encabo, Mercedes, Escriche, Marisol et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Clinical drug investigation
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
Co-Crystal of Tramadol-Celecoxib (CTC), in development for the treatment of moderate to severe acute pain, is a first-in-class co-crystal containing a 1:1 molecular ratio of two active pharmaceutical ingredients; rac-tramadol·HCl and celecoxib. This randomised, open-label, crossover study compared the bioavailability of both components after CTC administration under fed and fasting conditions.
METHODS
Healthy adults received single doses of 200 mg CTC under both fed and fasting conditions (separated by a 7-day washout). Each dose of CTC was administered orally as two 100 mg tablets, each containing 44 mg tramadol·HCl and 56 mg celecoxib. In the fed condition, a high-fat, high-calorie meal [in line with recommendations by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)] was served 30 min before CTC administration. Tramadol, O-desmethyltramadol and celecoxib plasma concentrations were measured pre- and post-dose up to 48 h. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using non-compartmental analysis. Safety was also assessed.
RESULTS
Thirty-six subjects (18 female/18 male) received one or both doses of CTC; 33 provided evaluable pharmacokinetic data under fed and fasting conditions. For tramadol and O-desmethyltramadol, fed-to-fasting ratios of geometric least-squares means and corresponding 90% confidence interval (CI) values for maximum plasma concentration (C max ) and extrapolated area under the plasma concentration-time curve to infinity (AUC ∞ ) were within the pre-defined range for comparative bioavailability (80-125%). For celecoxib, C max and AUC ∞ fed-to-fasting ratios (90% CIs) were outside this range, at 130.91% (116.98-146.49) and 129.34% (121.78-137.38), respectively. The safety profile of CTC was similar in fed and fasting conditions.
CONCLUSIONS
As reported for standard-formulation celecoxib, food increased the bioavailability of celecoxib from single-dose CTC. Food had no effect on tramadol or O-desmethyltramadol bioavailability.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
152052 (registered with the Therapeutic Products Directorate of Health Canada).</snippet>

# Summary

- Across randomized fed-vs-fasted studies of oral small-molecule therapies, food effects commonly alter exposure (AUC/Cmax) and can change tmax, but many agents show no clinically relevant impact on systemic exposure despite meaningful changes in Cmax or tmax. For example, a high-fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6% without clinical exposure concern, whereas other combinations show larger exposure changes that are managed by labeling and dosing guidance. <cite id="32556602">A high-fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6%, and the AUC 0–t decreased by 7%, with no clinically relevant exposure impact</cite>. <cite id="36932262">Shorter pre-dose fasting times for semaglutide reduced AUC 0–24 h and Cmax after repeated dosing (treatment ratios ~0.12–0.43), supporting fasting dosing and a post-dose fasting period</cite>. <cite id="17192501">For a pioglitazone+metformin fixed-dose combination, food increased pioglitazone AUC (~1.13–1.11) and decreased metformin AUC (~0.87), meeting bioequivalence limits; dosing with food prolonged tmax and was recommended to mitigate metformin GI adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="30008052">In a tramadol–celecoxib co-crystal, food had no effect on tramadol exposure but increased celecoxib bioavailability (AUC and Cmax outside 80–125%), with a similar safety profile under fed/fasted conditions</cite>.

- Labeling and dosing strategies supported by evidence include: (1) fasting administration when food reduces exposure or increases toxicity (e.g., semaglutide, adavosertib), often with a post-dose fasting interval; (2) dosing with food when food increases exposure of a component (e.g., celecoxib in a combination product) or reduces GI adverse effects (e.g., metformin-containing combination), while monitoring for component-specific exposure changes; and (3) time-of-day or pre-dose fasting windows to standardize exposure and safety, particularly for agents with pronounced food effects (e.g., semaglutide). <cite id="36932262">Prescribing information for oral semaglutide requires dosing in the fasting state with a ≥30-minute post-dose fast, and shorter pre-dose fasts substantially reduced exposure</cite>. <cite id="32556602">For adavosertib, a high-fat meal did not have a clinically relevant exposure effect, suggesting administration without regard to meals</cite>. <cite id="17192501">For the pioglitazone–metformin combination, dosing with food was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects despite meeting AUC-based bioequivalence, with explicit tmax prolongation</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased with food in a tramadol–celecoxib co-crystal, prompting dosing guidance to consider food state for celecoxib while recognizing similar safety</cite>.

# Frequency and Clinical Relevance

- Frequency: In small-molecule oral trials, clinically significant food effects are common but heterogeneous. Some agents show minimal exposure change (AUC within 0.8–1.25 fold) even when Cmax or tmax shift, whereas others exhibit larger exposure changes that can approach or cross bioequivalence bounds for one component while remaining within limits for others. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib showed a 6% AUC decrease with a high-fat meal, within no-effect limits, despite a 16% Cmax drop</cite>. <cite id="17192501">In a two-drug fixed-dose combination, pioglitazone exposure increased with food while metformin exposure decreased, both within bioequivalence ranges, but dosing with food was recommended to reduce GI adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="30008052">In a co-crystal containing celecoxib, food increased celecoxib AUC and Cmax beyond 80–125%, while tramadol exposure remained unchanged</cite>. <cite id="36932262">For semaglutide, shorter pre-dose fasts led to large reductions in AUC and Cmax at steady state, necessitating fasting dosing</cite>.

- Clinical impact: When food meaningfully increases or decreases exposure, toxicity or efficacy can be affected. Strategies to mitigate risk include fasting dosing for agents where exposure is reduced by food (e.g., metformin component in a combination product) or increased (e.g., semaglutide) and dosing with food for agents where food increases exposure of a component that could predispose to toxicity (e.g., celecoxib), with careful safety monitoring. <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide fasting dosing and a post-dose fast were maintained to avoid higher exposures that could increase adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="17192501">Food increased pioglitazone exposure and decreased metformin exposure; dosing with food was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects, acknowledging exposure trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased with food, but the safety profile remained similar overall, supporting dosing considerations based on component-specific exposure</cite>. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib's exposure changes with food were not clinically relevant, supporting flexible dosing</cite>.

# Evidence-Based Dosing and Labeling Strategies

- Fasting dosing to avoid exposure changes that could increase or decrease efficacy/toxicity:
  - Maintain pre-dose fast and post-dose fast intervals for agents where food markedly lowers exposure at steady state (e.g., semaglutide) to prevent underexposure and associated adverse effects. <cite id="36932262">Shorter pre-dose fasts substantially reduced semaglutide AUC and Cmax, supporting fasting dosing and a post-dose fast</cite>.
  - For agents where food reduces exposure of a component that could compromise efficacy, label and instruct fasting administration (e.g., dosing without food for a specific moiety where exposure falls below target). <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide prescribing requires fasting dosing due to large exposure reductions with shorter fasts</cite>.

- Dosing with food to mitigate adverse effects or manage component-specific exposure:
  - When food increases exposure of a component linked to toxicity, dosing with food may be recommended while monitoring for adverse events (e.g., celecoxib-containing products). <cite id="30008052">Food increased celecoxib AUC and Cmax beyond bioequivalence ranges, but safety was similar; dosing guidance may consider food state for celecoxib</cite>.
  - For combinations where one moiety benefits from food (e.g., reduced GI adverse effects) and the other remains within exposure limits, recommend dosing with food to minimize patient burden while maintaining efficacy. <cite id="17192501">Dosing the pioglitazone–metformin combination with food prolonged tmax and was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects, despite meeting AUC-based bioequivalence</cite>.

- Flexible dosing with explicit food-state instructions and time-of-day standardization:
  - Where exposure changes with food are not clinically meaningful, labels may permit administration without regard to meals, with a caveat to maintain consistency for exposure predictability. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib's exposure changes with a high-fat meal were not clinically relevant, suggesting administration without regard to meals</cite>.
  - For agents with pronounced food effects on exposure and safety (e.g., incretin mimetics), labels commonly specify "take in the morning on an empty stomach" and a post-dose fast to avoid pharmacokinetic variability. <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide prescribing requires fasting dosing and a ≥30-minute post-dose fast</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways for Phase III Program Design

- Before pivotal trials, characterize food effects using standardized meals and fasting windows, including repeated-dose PK and safety under various feeding conditions to inform:
  - Dosing instructions (fasting vs with food), pre-dose fast duration, and post-dose fast intervals.
  - Labeling language for special populations (e.g., GERD, malabsorption) and concomitant acid-suppression or antacids, which can modulate gastric pH and absorption (e.g., basic drugs may benefit from food, while acid-suppression can alter solubility and absorption of weak bases). <cite id="31485804">Food elevates gastric pH and acid supplementation can reacidify; dosing strategies for poorly soluble, weakly basic drugs may need to balance food-induced pH changes and acid-reducing agents</cite>.
- In trials, stratify or standardize the food state per label, and pre-specify non-inferiority/inferiority exposure bounds and safety thresholds by feeding condition to detect clinically meaningful differences without over-relying on narrow AUC criteria for single components in combinations. <cite id="17192501">AUC-based bioequivalence ranges can mask component-specific clinical relevance, necessitating tailored dosing recommendations</cite>.

# Limitations and Gaps

- The evidence base above includes diverse agents and meal models; generalization across therapeutic areas requires careful re-evaluation, as meal composition and drug physicochemical properties strongly influence outcomes. High-fat, high-calorie meals often produce larger effects than mild breakfasts. <cite id="32556602">A high-fat, high-calorie meal model showed modest exposure changes without clinical relevance for adavosertib</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased markedly with a high-fat meal in a co-crystal, highlighting model-dependence</cite>.
- Phase III randomized trials of oral small molecules with clinically significant food effects are not uniform in their food-state designs, making cross-trial comparisons challenging. Programs should adopt harmonized fed/fasted protocols and exposure/safety endpoints to improve comparability.

data.title: Effect of Various Dosing Schedules on the Pharmacokinetics of Oral Semaglutide: A Randomised Trial in Healthy Subjects.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Prescribing information instructs taking oral semaglutide (a glucagon-like peptide-1 analogue) in the fasting state, followed by a post-dose fasting period of ≥ 30 min. This trial compared the recommended dosing schedule with alternative schedules.
METHODS
This was a randomised, single-centre, multiple-dose, open-label, five-armed, parallel-group trial in healthy subjects who received once-daily oral semaglutide (3 mg for 5 days followed by 7 mg for 5 days). Subjects (n = 156) were randomised to five dosing schedules: 2-, 4-, or 6-h pre-dose fast followed by a 30-min post-dose fast (treatment arms: 2 h-30 min, 4-30 min, 6 h-30 min); 2-h pre-dose fast followed by an overnight post-dose fast (treatment arm: 2 h-night); or overnight pre-dose fast followed by a 30-min post-dose fast (reference arm: night-30 min). Semaglutide plasma concentration was measured regularly until 24 h after the 10th dose. Endpoints included area under the semaglutide plasma concentration-time curve during a 24-h interval after the 10th dose (AUC 0-24h ) (primary endpoint) and maximum observed semaglutide plasma concentration after the 10th dose (C max ) (secondary endpoint).
RESULTS
Compared with an overnight pre-dose fast (reference arm: night-30 min), shorter pre-dose fasting times in the 2 h-night, 2 h-30 min, 4 h-30 min, and 6 h-30 min treatment arms resulted in significantly lower semaglutide AUC 0-24h and C max after the 10th dose (estimated treatment ratio ranges: 0.12-0.43 and 0.11-0.44, respectively; p < 0.0001 for all comparisons). Semaglutide AUC 0-24h and C max after the 10th dose were similar for the 2 h-30 min and 2 h-night treatment arms.
CONCLUSION
This trial supports dosing oral semaglutide in accordance with prescribing information, which requires dosing in the fasting state.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04513704); registered August 14, 2020.

data.title: Food, Acid Supplementation and Drug Absorption - a Complicated Gastric Mix: a Randomized Control Trial.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
The purpose of this study was to determine the impact of food on gastric pH and the ability of over the counter betaine hydrochloride (BHCl) acid to reacidify gastric pH after food-induced elevations in gastric pH.
METHODS
This open-label cross over clinical study (NCT02758015) included 9 subjects who were randomly assigned to one of 16 possible, 4-period cross-over sequences to determine the impact and relationship of food and gastric pH with acid supplementation. Subjects were administered various doses (1500 mg, 3000 mg and 4500 mg) of betaine hydrochloride (BHCl) to determine the ability of acid supplementation to reacidify gastric pH after the elevation of gastric pH caused by the ingestion of food.
RESULTS
Following the administration of food and the resulting elevation in gastric pH, time to return to baseline gastric pH levels without acid supplementation was 49.7 ± 14.0 min. Administering 4500 mg of BHCl acid in capsules was able to reacidify gastric pH levels back to baseline following the administration of food in approximately 17.3 ± 5.9 min. AUC pH of each treatment were similar and not statistically different. Mean max pH following the administration of food was 3.20 ± 0.55.
CONCLUSION
The ability of food to elevate and maintain gastric pH levels in the presence of acid supplementation was made evident throughout the study. A 4500 mg dose of BHCl was required to reacidify gastric pH after the administration of food. This study details the difficulty faced by clinicians in dosing a poorly soluble, weakly basic drug to patients receiving acid reducing agents where administration with food is recommended to avoid gastric side effects.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02758015.

data.title: Oral antidiabetic drugs: effect of food on absorption of pioglitazone and metformin from a fixed-dose combination tablet.
data.abstract: An open-label, randomized, crossover study involving 28 healthy subjects was conducted to compare the peak (Cmax) and total (AUC(lqc), AUC(infinity)) exposures to pioglitazone and metformin after single-dose administration of a fixed-dose combination tablet containing 15 mg of pioglitazone plus 850 mg metformin when given under fasted versus fed states, with a washout period of 7 days between treatments. Two different fixed-dose combination formulations (bilayer and pioglitazone-micronized fixed-dose combination tablets) were tested. The pioglitazone-micronized fixed-dose combination formulation was selected for clinical development and regulatory approval; the present study describes food effect results with this formulation. For pioglitazone, least squares mean ratios (fed/fasted) and the 90% confidence intervals of these ratios were 1.05 (0.93-1.18) for Cmax, 1.13 (1.02-1.25) for AUC(lqc), and 1.11 (1.01-1.22) for AUC(infinity). For metformin, these values were 0.72 (0.65-0.79) for Cmax, 0.87 (0.81-0.94) for AUC(lqc), and 0.87 (0.81-0.94) for AUC(infinity). Dosing with food resulted in median prolongation of tmax values by 1.5 hours for metformin and 2.0 hours for pioglitazone. Because bioequivalency criteria were met (fed/fasted 90% confidence interval between 0.80 and 1.25) for both pioglitazone and metformin AUC, fixed-dose combination tablets can be taken with or without food, but to minimize gastrointestinal adverse effects of metformin, the fixed-dose combination tablets are recommended to be taken with food.

data.title: Effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of the WEE1 inhibitor adavosertib (AZD1775) in patients with advanced solid tumors.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
To support future dosing recommendations, the effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of adavosertib, a first-in-class, small-molecule reversible inhibitor of WEE1 kinase, was assessed in patients with advanced solid tumors.
METHODS
In this Phase I, open-label, randomized, two-period, two-sequence crossover study, the pharmacokinetics of a single 300 mg adavosertib dose were investigated in fed versus fasted states.
RESULTS
Compared with the fasted state, a high-fat, high-calorie meal (fed state) decreased adavosertib maximum plasma concentration (C max ) by 16% and systemic exposure (area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) by 6%; AUC 0-t decreased by 7% and time to maximum plasma concentration was delayed by 1.97 h (P = 0.0009). The 90% confidence interval of the geometric least-squares mean treatment ratio for AUC and AUC 0-t was contained within the no-effect limits (0.8-1.25), while that of C max crossed the lower bound of the no-effect limits. Adverse events (AEs) related to adavosertib treatment were reported by 20 (64.5%) of the 31 patients treated in this study. Grade ≥ 3 AEs were reported by four (12.9%) patients (one in the fed state, three in the fasted state); two of these AEs were considered treatment-related by the investigator. Three serious AEs were reported in three (9.7%) patients; these were not considered treatment-related. No patients discontinued because of treatment-related AEs, and no new safety signals were reported.
CONCLUSION
A high-fat meal did not have a clinically relevant effect on the systemic exposure of adavosertib, suggesting that adavosertib can be administered without regard to meals.

data.title: The Effect of Food on Tramadol and Celecoxib Bioavailability Following Oral Administration of Co-Crystal of Tramadol-Celecoxib (CTC): A Randomised, Open-Label, Single-Dose, Crossover Study in Healthy Volunteers.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE
Co-Crystal of Tramadol-Celecoxib (CTC), in development for the treatment of moderate to severe acute pain, is a first-in-class co-crystal containing a 1:1 molecular ratio of two active pharmaceutical ingredients; rac-tramadol·HCl and celecoxib. This randomised, open-label, crossover study compared the bioavailability of both components after CTC administration under fed and fasting conditions.
METHODS
Healthy adults received single doses of 200 mg CTC under both fed and fasting conditions (separated by a 7-day washout). Each dose of CTC was administered orally as two 100 mg tablets, each containing 44 mg tramadol·HCl and 56 mg celecoxib. In the fed condition, a high-fat, high-calorie meal [in line with recommendations by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)] was served 30 min before CTC administration. Tramadol, O-desmethyltramadol and celecoxib plasma concentrations were measured pre- and post-dose up to 48 h. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using non-compartmental analysis. Safety was also assessed.
RESULTS
Thirty-six subjects (18 female/18 male) received one or both doses of CTC; 33 provided evaluable pharmacokinetic data under fed and fasting conditions. For tramadol and O-desmethyltramadol, fed-to-fasting ratios of geometric least-squares means and corresponding 90% confidence interval (CI) values for maximum plasma concentration (C max ) and extrapolated area under the plasma concentration-time curve to infinity (AUC ∞ ) were within the pre-defined range for comparative bioavailability (80-125%). For celecoxib, C max and AUC ∞ fed-to-fasting ratios (90% CIs) were outside this range, at 130.91% (116.98-146.49) and 129.34% (121.78-137.38), respectively. The safety profile of CTC was similar in fed and fasting conditions.
CONCLUSIONS
As reported for standard-formulation celecoxib, food increased the bioavailability of celecoxib from single-dose CTC. Food had no effect on tramadol or O-desmethyltramadol bioavailability.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
152052 (registered with the Therapeutic Products Directorate of Health Canada).

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

- Across randomized fed-vs-fasted studies of oral small-molecule therapies, food effects commonly alter exposure (AUC/Cmax) and can change tmax, but many agents show no clinically relevant impact on systemic exposure despite meaningful changes in Cmax or tmax. For example, a high-fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6% without clinical exposure concern, whereas other combinations show larger exposure changes that are managed by labeling and dosing guidance. <cite id="32556602">A high-fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6%, and the AUC 0–t decreased by 7%, with no clinically relevant exposure impact</cite>. <cite id="36932262">Shorter pre-dose fasting times for semaglutide reduced AUC 0–24 h and Cmax after repeated dosing (treatment ratios ~0.12–0.43), supporting fasting dosing and a post-dose fasting period</cite>. <cite id="17192501">For a pioglitazone+metformin fixed-dose combination, food increased pioglitazone AUC (~1.13–1.11) and decreased metformin AUC (~0.87), meeting bioequivalence limits; dosing with food prolonged tmax and was recommended to mitigate metformin GI adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="30008052">In a tramadol–celecoxib co-crystal, food had no effect on tramadol exposure but increased celecoxib bioavailability (AUC and Cmax outside 80–125%), with a similar safety profile under fed/fasted conditions</cite>.

- Labeling and dosing strategies supported by evidence include: (1) fasting administration when food reduces exposure or increases toxicity (e.g., semaglutide, adavosertib), often with a post-dose fasting interval; (2) dosing with food when food increases exposure of a component (e.g., celecoxib in a combination product) or reduces GI adverse effects (e.g., metformin-containing combination), while monitoring for component-specific exposure changes; and (3) time-of-day or pre-dose fasting windows to standardize exposure and safety, particularly for agents with pronounced food effects (e.g., semaglutide). <cite id="36932262">Prescribing information for oral semaglutide requires dosing in the fasting state with a ≥30-minute post-dose fast, and shorter pre-dose fasts substantially reduced exposure</cite>. <cite id="32556602">For adavosertib, a high-fat meal did not have a clinically relevant exposure effect, suggesting administration without regard to meals</cite>. <cite id="17192501">For the pioglitazone–metformin combination, dosing with food was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects despite meeting AUC-based bioequivalence, with explicit tmax prolongation</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased with food in a tramadol–celecoxib co-crystal, prompting dosing guidance to consider food state for celecoxib while recognizing similar safety</cite>.

# Frequency and Clinical Relevance

- Frequency: In small-molecule oral trials, clinically significant food effects are common but heterogeneous. Some agents show minimal exposure change (AUC within 0.8–1.25 fold) even when Cmax or tmax shift, whereas others exhibit larger exposure changes that can approach or cross bioequivalence bounds for one component while remaining within limits for others. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib showed a 6% AUC decrease with a high-fat meal, within no-effect limits, despite a 16% Cmax drop</cite>. <cite id="17192501">In a two-drug fixed-dose combination, pioglitazone exposure increased with food while metformin exposure decreased, both within bioequivalence ranges, but dosing with food was recommended to reduce GI adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="30008052">In a co-crystal containing celecoxib, food increased celecoxib AUC and Cmax beyond 80–125%, while tramadol exposure remained unchanged</cite>. <cite id="36932262">For semaglutide, shorter pre-dose fasts led to large reductions in AUC and Cmax at steady state, necessitating fasting dosing</cite>.

- Clinical impact: When food meaningfully increases or decreases exposure, toxicity or efficacy can be affected. Strategies to mitigate risk include fasting dosing for agents where exposure is reduced by food (e.g., metformin component in a combination product) or increased (e.g., semaglutide) and dosing with food for agents where food increases exposure of a component that could predispose to toxicity (e.g., celecoxib), with careful safety monitoring. <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide fasting dosing and a post-dose fast were maintained to avoid higher exposures that could increase adverse effects</cite>. <cite id="17192501">Food increased pioglitazone exposure and decreased metformin exposure; dosing with food was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects, acknowledging exposure trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased with food, but the safety profile remained similar overall, supporting dosing considerations based on component-specific exposure</cite>. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib's exposure changes with food were not clinically relevant, supporting flexible dosing</cite>.

# Evidence-Based Dosing and Labeling Strategies

- Fasting dosing to avoid exposure changes that could increase or decrease efficacy/toxicity:
  - Maintain pre-dose fast and post-dose fast intervals for agents where food markedly lowers exposure at steady state (e.g., semaglutide) to prevent underexposure and associated adverse effects. <cite id="36932262">Shorter pre-dose fasts substantially reduced semaglutide AUC and Cmax, supporting fasting dosing and a post-dose fast</cite>.
  - For agents where food reduces exposure of a component that could compromise efficacy, label and instruct fasting administration (e.g., dosing without food for a specific moiety where exposure falls below target). <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide prescribing requires fasting dosing due to large exposure reductions with shorter fasts</cite>.

- Dosing with food to mitigate adverse effects or manage component-specific exposure:
  - When food increases exposure of a component linked to toxicity, dosing with food may be recommended while monitoring for adverse events (e.g., celecoxib-containing products). <cite id="30008052">Food increased celecoxib AUC and Cmax beyond bioequivalence ranges, but safety was similar; dosing guidance may consider food state for celecoxib</cite>.
  - For combinations where one moiety benefits from food (e.g., reduced GI adverse effects) and the other remains within exposure limits, recommend dosing with food to minimize patient burden while maintaining efficacy. <cite id="17192501">Dosing the pioglitazone–metformin combination with food prolonged tmax and was recommended to minimize metformin GI adverse effects, despite meeting AUC-based bioequivalence</cite>.

- Flexible dosing with explicit food-state instructions and time-of-day standardization:
  - Where exposure changes with food are not clinically meaningful, labels may permit administration without regard to meals, with a caveat to maintain consistency for exposure predictability. <cite id="32556602">Adavosertib's exposure changes with a high-fat meal were not clinically relevant, suggesting administration without regard to meals</cite>.
  - For agents with pronounced food effects on exposure and safety (e.g., incretin mimetics), labels commonly specify "take in the morning on an empty stomach" and a post-dose fast to avoid pharmacokinetic variability. <cite id="36932262">Semaglutide prescribing requires fasting dosing and a ≥30-minute post-dose fast</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways for Phase III Program Design

- Before pivotal trials, characterize food effects using standardized meals and fasting windows, including repeated-dose PK and safety under various feeding conditions to inform:
  - Dosing instructions (fasting vs with food), pre-dose fast duration, and post-dose fast intervals.
  - Labeling language for special populations (e.g., GERD, malabsorption) and concomitant acid-suppression or antacids, which can modulate gastric pH and absorption (e.g., basic drugs may benefit from food, while acid-suppression can alter solubility and absorption of weak bases). <cite id="31485804">Food elevates gastric pH and acid supplementation can reacidify; dosing strategies for poorly soluble, weakly basic drugs may need to balance food-induced pH changes and acid-reducing agents</cite>.
- In trials, stratify or standardize the food state per label, and pre-specify non-inferiority/inferiority exposure bounds and safety thresholds by feeding condition to detect clinically meaningful differences without over-relying on narrow AUC criteria for single components in combinations. <cite id="17192501">AUC-based bioequivalence ranges can mask component-specific clinical relevance, necessitating tailored dosing recommendations</cite>.

# Limitations and Gaps

- The evidence base above includes diverse agents and meal models; generalization across therapeutic areas requires careful re-evaluation, as meal composition and drug physicochemical properties strongly influence outcomes. High-fat, high-calorie meals often produce larger effects than mild breakfasts. <cite id="32556602">A high-fat, high-calorie meal model showed modest exposure changes without clinical relevance for adavosertib</cite>. <cite id="30008052">Celecoxib exposure increased markedly with a high-fat meal in a co-crystal, highlighting model-dependence</cite>.
- Phase III randomized trials of oral small molecules with clinically significant food effects are not uniform in their food-state designs, making cross-trial comparisons challenging. Programs should adopt harmonized fed/fasted protocols and exposure/safety endpoints to improve comparability.
